title: Explainer-Who are the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen?
gist: A Reuters explainer published by Al-Monitor on Oct. 4, 2026: Yemen's Saudi-backed government launched a counteroffensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, reigniting a civil war frozen since the 2022 UN truce and raising Red Sea shipping risk at a time when Iran has mostly choked off the Strait of Hormuz, compounding a global oil crisis; it also outlines Houthi origins, capabilities and their looser-than-proxy ties to Iran.

themes.theme: Renewed Yemen war and energy-route risk

insights.claim: Yemen's Saudi-backed government announced the start of a military counteroffensive against the Iran-backed Houthis aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Opens a second active front around Gulf energy routes, adding to supply-disruption risk.
insights.quote: announced the start of a military counteroffensive against the Iran-backed Houthis

insights.claim: Renewed Houthi-Saudi warfare has reignited Yemen's frozen civil war and heightened risks to Red Sea shipping, further disrupting Middle Eastern energy exports already choked by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: With both Hormuz and the Red Sea at risk, alternative export routes (e.g., Saudi Red Sea ports) are also exposed, worsening the oil supply squeeze.
insights.quote: heightened risks to Red Sea shipping, further disrupting Middle Eastern energy exports already choked by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: Houthi threats to oil tankers during the Iran war have added to the squeeze on Gulf energy after Tehran mostly choked off the Strait of Hormuz, contributing to a global oil crisis.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Supports elevated oil prices and tanker freight/insurance costs while both chokepoints are contested.
insights.quote: adding to a global oil crisis
insights.locator: HOW MUCH DAMAGE CAN THE HOUTHIS DO

insights.claim: Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023-2025 significantly disrupted global trade, forcing Europe-Asia cargo ships onto a long, expensive route around Africa; attacks on shipping and Saudi Arabia resumed this year in response to the US war on Iran.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Precedent implies renewed Suez-route avoidance, higher container freight rates and longer transit times.
insights.quote: forcing cargo ships travelling between Europe and Asia to take a long, expensive route around Africa
insights.locator: HOW MUCH DAMAGE CAN THE HOUTHIS DO

insights.claim: Houthi missile and drone attacks have caused significant damage in Saudi Arabia and the UAE, including on oil installations and vital infrastructure, but have proven less effective against more distant targets such as Israel.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Saudi and UAE energy infrastructure is the most exposed target set if the war escalates.
insights.quote: have proven less effective against targets further north, such as Israel
insights.locator: Some Houthi missile and drone attacks

insights.claim: Despite a Saudi-led intervention since 2015 with years of airstrikes, neither side gained much ground in Yemen's mountainous terrain and the Houthis kept control of the populous northwest.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: History suggests the new counteroffensive may struggle to deliver a decisive outcome, implying a prolonged conflict.
insights.quote: neither side was able to gain much ground in Yemen's mountainous terrain

insights.claim: The Houthis emerged in the 1990s as a Zaydi Shi'ite revival movement, consolidated control of northern Yemen after Ali Abdullah Saleh's 2011 fall, grew under Abdul Malik al-Houthi into a force of tens of thousands with Iranian support, and seized Sanaa in 2014.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: An entrenched, locally rooted movement is unlikely to be dislodged quickly.

insights.claim: A UN-brokered 2022 truce maintained peace in Yemen until this year.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: The collapse of a multi-year truce marks a regime shift in Yemen risk.
insights.quote: the UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that maintained peace until this year
insights.locator: After years of fighting, the UN brokered

insights.claim: Although Iran champions the Houthis as part of its Axis of Resistance alongside Hezbollah and Iraqi Shi'ite militias, its ties with the Houthis are less clear: the Houthis do not recognize Iran's supreme leader as ultimate religious authority and their motivations are mainly domestic.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Houthi behavior may not de-escalate in lockstep with any US-Iran deal, so Red Sea risk could outlast Hormuz risk.
insights.quote: Their motivations are also mainly domestic, though they are ideologically aligned with Iran.

insights.claim: The US says Iran has armed, funded and trained the Houthis with help from Hezbollah, while the Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy and say they develop their own weapons.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Contested attribution affects whether Houthi attacks are treated as Iranian escalation by Washington.
insights.quote: The Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy and say they develop their own weapons.
